vignette:
She is seventy-one now, composed in the way people often become after a lifetime of working with numbers, but there are moments in session when her face changes and she looks much younger, almost startled by something only she can see. She works as a financial analyst for a small regional firm, long past the age when many of her peers have retired. She says work gives her structure. "Columns behave," she says with a brief smile. "If something is off, you can find where." What does not behave, what does not stay in any neat column, is what happened to her decades ago.

She grows up in Southeast Asia in a large family where everyone knows everyone else's business and where a young woman learns early to be useful, quiet, and alert to the moods around her. In her late twenties, during a period of political upheaval, she is taken along with others by armed men while traveling between towns. Even now she does not tell that part quickly. She reaches it in pieces, circling around it before she can say plainly that she is held captive for weeks in a dark, crowded place she cannot leave. There is no clock, no privacy, no certainty about food or water, only commands shouted by men whose footsteps she learns to recognize before she sees them. She remembers most vividly the loss of ordinary choices: when to stand, when to sleep, when to use the toilet, when to speak. She learns to make herself small. She counts breaths to pass the time. She mentally recites multiplication tables and household inventories, as if keeping track of facts might keep her mind intact.

During captivity she begins to live in a state of constant anticipation. Every sound means something. Every pause in the hallway feels dangerous. She watches others for clues and trusts no sign of calm. Once released, she expects relief to come immediately, but instead she feels wrong in the world, as if her body has remained behind. People tell her she is lucky to be alive. She nods and says thank you. Inside, she feels ashamed that she survived by obeying, ashamed of how frightened she still is. At night she startles awake certain she has heard boots outside her door. For years she sleeps lightly, fully dressed or with her shoes beside the bed. If a room has no visible exit, she cannot settle in it.

After immigrating to the United States, she builds a life that looks admirable from the outside. She studies, works hard, marries, has a daughter, divorces later without much drama. She develops a reputation at work for precision and calm. She likes spreadsheets because they reward vigilance, and because checking and rechecking numbers is seen as competence rather than fear. Colleagues know her as dependable, maybe a little formal. They do not know that she arrives early so she can choose a seat facing the door, or that she keeps snacks in every drawer because hunger makes her panicky in a way she cannot explain. When office renovations temporarily move her team into a windowless conference room, she tells her supervisor she needs another workspace because of "concentration issues," then spends lunch in her car with the engine running until her hands stop shaking.

She does not think of herself as someone who talks about feelings. For many years, she avoids reminders with the same discipline she uses at work. She does not watch war films. She does not go to crowded basements or locked interior rooms. She skips community events if security personnel are present with radios on their belts. On bad nights she dreams she is back in captivity, unable to move freely, unable to protect herself. She wakes disoriented, heart pounding, and for a few seconds the bedroom is not her bedroom. Those mornings she is irritable and exacting with everyone. She knows this. She hates it. If her adult daughter drops by unexpectedly and stands too close behind her in the kitchen, she spins around sharply before she can stop herself, one hand pressed to her chest, embarrassed by the fear in her own house.

As she ages, the old strategies seem less reliable. Retirement conversations at work stir up more anxiety than she expects; without the routine of financial reports and quarterly deadlines, she worries there will be too much room for memories. After a minor incident in an elevator that stalls between floors for less than five minutes, she cannot bring herself to use elevators for months. She takes the stairs even when her knees ache. She notices herself scanning hallways, memorizing exits, listening for footsteps in a way that feels automatic and exhausting. Some afternoons, while reviewing budgets, she loses track of a simple formula because she has drifted into a vivid recollection of dim walls, stale air, and the sound of someone crying nearby. Then she becomes angry with herself for "still being this way."

In session, she often minimizes first and then reveals more. She says she should be grateful, that others suffered worse, that she has had a successful life. All of that is true, and still she lives as though captivity remains a possibility at any moment. She keeps her phone charged, her pantry overstocked, her blinds adjusted just so. She sits nearest the door in my office and notices every sound in the corridor. When she describes herself, she usually starts with practical roles-mother, analyst, immigrant, divorcée-but over time another truth emerges: much of her life has been organized around never again being trapped.
